 The Economist launches The World Ahead 2027: heralding the post-Trump era, amid upheaval from bond markets and AI The Economist launches The World Ahead 2027: heralding the post-Trump era, amid upheaval from bond markets and AI
 London, United Kingdom November 17, 2026 
 Main Content 
 The Economist has today launched The World Ahead , its annual future-gazing report analysing the themes that will prove most consequential in the coming year. 
 Political and financial shocks seem likely, and AI-led turmoil appears all but certain. The backlash against big tech firms will grow, as worries grow about the impact of artificial intelligence.
 As always, journalists from The Economist are joined by a diverse range of political, academic, and business voices, with contributing articles from presidents, prime ministers, industry leaders and eminent scholars of history and science.
 “He won’t be a lame duck - more like a destructive Angry Bird” 
 Commenting on this year’s edition of The World Ahead , its editor, Tom Standage, said: “The post-Trump era is beginning. But don’t expect the president to go quietly. With Democrats taking charge of both chambers of Congress, Donald Trump will, if anything, become even more aggressive and mercurial. Expect more executive orders, legal spats, sudden renamings of geographical features, grandiose building projects and military adventures as he furiously tries to retain his influence and shape his legacy.”
 “Elsewhere, the world will grapple with aftershocks from the Iran war, as fertiliser shortages and a super El Niño threaten food security for millions. The political, financial and cyber risks associated with AI will become ever more apparent as its capabilities grow. In Europe, the big question will be whether voters in France elect Marine Le Pen as their next president. That would cause a political earthquake in the EU, and would also spook bond markets, which are already concerned about France’s unsustainable fiscal position.”
 The World Ahead 2027 will be included in The Economist ’s weekly print edition dated November 21st, as well as being sold as a stand-alone newsstand edition from November 26th. Articles exploring the top ten themes for the coming year are online today at www.economist.com and cover the following topics:
 The post-Trump era: As the race to succeed him begins, the president won’t be a lame duck—more like a destructive Angry Bird. The world will start to wonder what a post-Trump America might look like.
 Aftershocks from Iran: America's allies no longer trust it and its enemies no longer fear it. The war's consequences will reshape regional politics, reconfigure energy flows and threaten food security, with fertiliser in short supply.
 Hottest year ever, again: Expect another year of droughts, wildfires and heat waves. Yet Mr Trump has unwittingly become the world's greatest salesman for renewable energy. It's the best way not just to address climate change, but to escape from the ups and downs of global energy markets.
 The AI backlash grows: The danger of a crash will rise, as Al firms take on more debt in complex, opaque deals. But while worries about AI’s political, financial and cyber risks are justified, concerns about its impact on jobs and the environment are overstated. 
 Europe's populist right: Victory for Marine le Pen would throw a spanner into the Franco-German engine that powers the European Union, and heighten concerns about debt-laden France's precarious public finances.
 Bond-market pressure: And it’s not just France. Many rich countries are living beyond their means, and bond yields are rising. This can't go on forever. Something, somewhere, has to break.
 Taiwan's moment of peril: Xi Jinping is said to have set a deadline of 2027 for China’s armed forces to be ready to capture the island. But technology has changed the nature of war, making it easier for smaller powers to fend off larger ones, as seen in Ukraine and Iran. How will that affect China’s designs on Taiwan?
 The Ozempic effect: As well as helping people lose weight, slimming drugs are changing consumer behaviour, with the newly slender splurging on clothes, cosmetics and fitness. At the same time, the drugs’ anti-ageing effects have rejuvenated pharma companies’ interest in longevity treatments.
 Cheaper space launch: SpaceX’s Starship will start making regular satellite launches,the first private-sector space station will launch, and the idea of building data centres in orbit will start to sound less crazy.
 Rebooting Hollywood: Star Wars is just one of the franchises trying to reach out to new audiences. But given the success of low-budget movies made by YouTubers, do audiences want something new? Perhaps. But with its depiction of a military superpower humbled by small, cheap craft, and misbehaving droids with their own agendas, Star Wars may be more relevant than ever in 2027.
 This year’s guest authors are:
 Takaichi Sanae , prime minister of Japan; Alexander Stubb , president of Finland; Jack Clark , co-founder and head of public benefit at Anthropic; Fatih Birol, head of the International Energy Agency; Kemi Badenoch , leader of the UK Conservative party; Odd Arne Westad , professor of history at Yale University; Bob Mumgaard , co-founder and CEO of Commonwealth Fusion Systems; He Xiaopeng , chairman and chief executive of Xpeng; and Terence Tao , professor of mathematics at UCLA.

 About The Economist 
 With rigorous reporting, in-depth analysis and global perspective, The Economist explains today’s most important events and seeks to discern the trends that will shape the future. In addition to the weekly print edition, The Economist publishes its journalism daily through its website, app, podcasts, newsletters and videos. The Economist has 1.3m subscribers.
